blocks.text: There are two different questions hiding in "when do I use a tree?". One is about **designing** a program: when should your data *live* in a tree? The other is about **interviews**: the tree is given — which way should you *walk* it? This lesson answers both.
When your data belongs in a tree

items: **It's hierarchical** — things contain things: folders, menus, comments with replies, an organisation chart.

**You need order and fast updates together** — a sorted array searches fast but inserts slowly; a hash table is fast but unordered. A **balanced binary search tree** gives O(log n) for search, insert, delete *and* min/max/range queries.
**You always need the smallest or largest item** — a **heap**, a complete binary tree stored in an array, gives the minimum in O(1) and updates in O(log n).
**You search by prefix** — a **trie** (a tree of characters) powers autocomplete.
**You're representing structure** — expressions, syntax, decisions, game moves.

blocks.alt: A decision list for choosing a structure. Does your data contain other data? Use a tree. Do you need sorted order plus fast inserts and deletes? Use a balanced binary search tree. Do you keep asking for the smallest or largest item? Use a heap. Do you only look things up by exact key? Use a hash map. Do you only add and remove at the ends? Use a stack or queue.

blocks.text: When a problem is a tree problem

In interviews the tree is usually given, and the words give it away: **root, leaf, subtree, ancestor, level, depth, path from the root**. Almost every such problem is "visit every node and do something" — so the real decision is **how to walk**:

blocks.alt: Two ways to walk the same tree. Depth-first search follows one branch all the way down before backing up: 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6, 7. Breadth-first search visits level by level: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

elements.text: depth-first (DFS): one branch at a time
elements.originalText: depth-first (DFS): one branch at a time

items: **Use depth-first search (DFS)** when a node's answer is built from its **subtrees**: heights, sums, "is it balanced", paths from the root to a leaf, lowest common ancestor. DFS is usually written with **recursion**; under the hood it's a **stack**.

**Use breadth-first search (BFS)** when the question is about **levels**: level order, averages per level, left/right/top views, the shallowest leaf, "are these two nodes on the same level". BFS uses a **queue**.

blocks.text: The two are the same loop. Swap the stack for a queue and the visiting order changes from "deep first" to "level by level":

blocks.caption: Run it on the deep-left tree: DFS dives straight down, BFS sweeps across.

blocks.text: Both visit every node once: **O(n) time**. Their memory differs: DFS holds about one root-to-leaf path, **O(h)**; BFS holds about one level, **O(w)**. Tall, thin trees favour BFS; wide, bushy trees favour DFS.
When a tree is the wrong tool

items: **You need the k-th item by position, instantly** — use an **array**.
**You only ever look up exact keys** and never need order — a **hash map** is simpler and faster on average.
**You only add and remove at the ends** — a **stack** or **queue** is all you need.
**Your data really is a sequence** — forcing it into a tree adds pointers and complexity for nothing.
Store data in a tree when it's **hierarchical**, or when you need **sorted order with fast updates** (balanced BST), **repeated min/max** (heap) or **prefix search** (trie).
Tree interview problems are about **how to walk**: DFS when answers combine subtrees, BFS when the question is about levels.
DFS is a **stack** (often the call stack via recursion); BFS is a **queue**. Same loop, different container.
DFS uses **O(h)** memory, BFS **O(w)**; both take **O(n)** time.
